c.tagline: Djerba's whitewashed island capital of souks, seafront forts, and ancient synagogues.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hailing apps on Djerba; get around by metered yellow taxis (insist on the meter, or agree a price first) and shared louage minibuses that run set routes between the island's towns.

emergency.note: 197 reaches the national police/guard, 190 is the SAMU ambulance service, and 198 is Civil Protection (fire and rescue).

hood_landmark.Houmt Souk (Old Town): Borj El Ghazi Mustapha, Houmt Souk

avoid.reason: Expect persistent souk touts and tourist overcharging, with occasional pickpocketing in crowded market lanes.

hood_desc: The island's main town, a maze of whitewashed lanes, covered souks, old fondouk courtyards turned guesthouses, and the seafront Borj El Ghazi Mustapha fort; best for first-timers who want markets, history, and cafe life on foot.

A quiet inland village south of town famous for the ancient El Ghriba synagogue and the Djerbahood street-art murals painted across its houses; suits travelers drawn to heritage, art, and Djerba's layered Jewish and Berber culture.
Djerba's lively second town, known for its big weekly market, restaurants, and proximity to the resort strip; a good base for shopping, dining out, and beach access.
A calm stretch of the southeast coast lined with beach resorts, palm groves, and long sandy shore; ideal for a relaxed, all-inclusive-style seaside stay.
The island's main resort beach northeast of Houmt Souk, a long sweep of sand backed by thalasso spa hotels and water-sports; a quiet, sea-facing base close to town.
lodging: TUI Blue Palm Beach Palace Djerba
Radisson Blu Palace Resort & Thalasso Djerba

water.note: Drink bottled water; Djerba's tap water is brackish and not recommended.

transit.hours: Taxis and shared louages run through the day and early evening; service thins after dark, when taxis are the main option.
transit.note: There is no metro, tram, or rail on Djerba. Getting around means metered yellow taxis, shared louage minibuses between towns, and rental cars or scooters; the island connects to the mainland by the El Kantara causeway and the Ajim-Jorf ferry.
transit.pay: Taxi and louage fares are paid in cash (Tunisian dinars) to the driver; there is no transit card. Keep small notes handy.

bus: SNTRI intercity coaches to Tunis, Gabès and Medenine
Local buses and louage minibuses across the island
ferry: Ajim-Jorf car ferry to the Tunisian mainland (El Kantara causeway also links the island by road)
train: No rail on the island; nearest railhead is Gabès on the mainland

transit.m: Rental car pickup at the terminal

tip.r: Around 10% at restaurants is customary; small tips for guides, drivers, hotel staff and hammam attendants are expected.
